query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored heat treatment that transforms single-phase BCC NbMoTaW into an inverted dual-phase microstructure—comprising a continuous BCC matrix with discrete, fine B2 precipitates—will improve room-temperature ductility without compromising its excellent high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW in a single-phase BCC structure with very poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored heat treatment involving a high-temperature solutionizing step followed by controlled annealing and cooling to induce the formation of discrete B2 precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: The heat treatment parameters (temperature, time, and cooling rate) must be optimized to produce a fine, dispersed B2 phase while retaining the continuous BCC matrix. The procedure should be calibrated to avoid excessive coarsening of precipitates that could impair high-temperature properties.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of discrete B2 precipitates distributed in a continuous BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The discrete B2 precipitates are expected to act as barriers to rapid crack propagation and to facilitate the activation of additional deformation mechanisms at room temperature, thereby increasing ductility. Meanwhile, the continuous BCC matrix sustains high lattice stability and strength at elevated temperatures and is not anticipated to adversely affect irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated single-phase BCC NbMoTaW, the treated alloy will exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility while maintaining comparable high-temperature yield strength (e.g., performance at 1600 °C) and robust irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW with a single-phase BCC structure that exhibits excellent high-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The success of the intervention depends on achieving the correct volume fraction and distribution of the B2 precipitates; an excessive or coarse B2 phase might deteriorate high-temperature performance or alter defect migration under irradiation. Furthermore, the heat treatment window must avoid undesirable phase transformations beyond the B2 phase.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement in room-temperature ductility and the potential trade-offs affecting high-temperature properties and irradiation resistance depend on the precise heat treatment parameters. The interplay between precipitate size, spacing, and stability introduces uncertainty that requires experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW alloy samples: one set processed by the tailored heat treatment to induce the dual-phase BCC+B2 microstructure, and a control set remaining in the single-phase BCC state. Characterize their microstructures using TEM/SEM to confirm the presence and uniformity of discrete B2 precipitates. Then, subject both sets to mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1600 °C, and perform irradiation experiments (using, e.g., ion irradiation protocols) to assess irradiation-induced defect evolution.
measurements: Irradiation resistance parameters (defect density, phase stability via post-irradiation microstructural analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility over the control, or if there is a notable degradation in high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance (e.g., increased defect accumulation or phase instability), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory HEAs (RHEAs) stand out among various types of HEAs due to their unparalleled mechanical properties at high temperatures exceeding 800 °C, and even up to 1500 °C in some cases [,], making them viable options for high-temperature structural applications, outperforming typical Ni-based superalloys. Refractory high-entropy alloys, thanks to their high strength at high temperatures, high melting point, and high hardness brought by their resistance to friction and wear properties, may be used in aerospace engines, gas turbines, and the nuclear irradiation field. However, the reported literature has primarily centered on compression deformation investigations. For most RHEAs, due to their room-temperature brittleness, their tensile ductility is commonly negligible []. Therefore, improving the room-temperature plasticity of RHEAs is the premise of its high-temperature application.

As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The present work is the first demonstration of enhancing the ductility of high-strength BCC + B2 two-phase RHEAs by controlling their microstructure. For this, Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was selected, based on its low density (7.4 g/cm3) and previous reports of excellent room and high temperature yield strength. This alloy was cast, hot isostatically pressed (HIPed) and then homogenized at 1200 °C for 24hrs followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature. The resultant microstructure consists of two BCC phases (one of which is likely ordered, but this was not previously proven) with very similar lattice parameters that form a very fine, inter-woven baskteweave-like, nano-phase structure. Subsequently, this will be referred as Condition (1). The alloy has a room-temperature yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compression strain before fracture in Condition (1). The present study focuses on improving the ductility of this alloy by tuning the microstructure, while maintaining its high yield strength. reading.lever: Apply a tailored heat treatment to convert NbMoTaW’s single-phase BCC structure into a dual-phase inverted BCC+B2 microstructure with discrete precipitates.
reading.why: This processing route, proven in related RHEAs, directly targets improving room-temperature ductility while preserving high-temperature strength and likely irradiation resistance.
